While courts may uphold nationwide non-competes in the context of stock purchase transactions, Saharia should negotiate to limit the area to regions where the Company actually conducts business or has customers, which would be more defensible and less burdensome.
issues.revision: The "Restricted Area" shall mean the United States, its territories andthose states within the United States in which the Company conducts business or has Customers as of the date of this Agreement.
issues.comment: Michigan courts require non-compete restrictions to be reasonable in geographic scope; limiting the Restricted Area to states where the Company actually conducts business or has customers ensures enforceability and avoids overbreadth that could void the restriction entirely.

issues.title: No Carve-Out for Activities in India
issues.description: The non-compete  restricts the Shareholder from "directly or indirectly" engaging in competitive activity in the Restricted Area. Since Saharia resides in India  and the business involves offshore services, even work performed in India that touches U.S. customers could arguably fall within this restriction through the "indirectly" language. Consider adding an express carve-out for activities conducted entirely outside the Restricted Area that do not target U.S. customers.

issues.title: Invalid subsection reference to Section 5(J)
issues.description: The Notices provision  contains a self-reference to "this Section 5(J)", but the Notices subsection appears to be Section 5(I), not Section 5(J). Based on the sequential lettering of subsections in Section 5, the Notices provision  is the ninth subsection (I), not the tenth (J). Only subsection A is explicitly labeled , but counting the subsequent provisions shows: A (Entire Agreement), B (No Waiver), C (Amendment), D (Representation), E (Governing Law), F (Successors and Assigns), G (Counterparts), H (Partial Invalidity), and I (Notices).

issues.title: Undefined term: Acquired Companies
issues.description: The term "Acquired Companies" and its singular form "Acquired Company" are used in the definition of Customer  but are never defined in the Agreement. This creates ambiguity about which entities are included when determining who qualifies as a Customer, particularly for purposes of the non-solicitation restrictions in Section 2. Given that Customer restrictions are a key part of the noncompetition obligations, the undefined nature of "Acquired Companies" undermines enforceability.

judgments.title: Passive Investment Threshold Too High
judgments.reason: The 2% threshold is definite; the issue concerns the commercial adequacy of that negotiated percentage, not textual construction.

judgments.title: Employee Non-Solicit Missing Independent Contractors
judgments.reason: The scope of “consultant” may be uncertain as applied to independent contractors, since some—but not necessarily all—independent contractors could reasonably fall within that term.

judgments.title: Punctuation error
judgments.reason: The period after “and” interrupts the coordinated phrase “promote and preserve,” leaving a grammatically malformed sentence and constituting a mechanical punctuation error.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Acquired Companies
judgments.reason: Although “Acquired Companies” is not defined within this document, Background C imports meanings for otherwise undefined capitalized terms from the Stock Purchase Agreement. The issue therefore does not establish an intrinsic ambiguity in this instrument.

judgments.title: Passive Investment Threshold Too Low at 2%
judgments.reason: The less-than-2% threshold is definite; whether market practice favors 5% is a negotiation issue.

judgments.title: Restricted Area Covers Entire United States

judgments.title: Injunctive Relief Without Bond Requirement
judgments.reason: The bond waiver is express and unambiguous. Its procedural fairness or enforceability does not create one of the specified construction defects.

judgments.title: Vague Notice Obligation for Compelled Disclosure
judgments.reason: “Adequate opportunity” is vague because the provision supplies no objective timing or procedural standard for determining adequacy.

judgments.title: Confidentiality Obligation Has No Time Limitation
judgments.reason: “At any time” during or after the Restricted Period clearly creates an indefinite obligation. The issue concerns reasonableness and enforceability, not uncertain meaning.

judgments.title: No Return or Destruction of Confidential Information
judgments.reason: A return-or-destruction obligation is simply absent; its omission does not make the existing nondisclosure and nonuse duties ambiguous.

judgments.title: Confidentiality Bond Waiver (Section 3)
judgments.reason: The confidentiality bond waiver is explicit; objecting to the allocation of procedural risk is a negotiation issue.

judgments.title: No Disparagement Exception Too Broad
judgments.reason: The phrase “as part of any dispute resolution proceeding” has an uncertain boundary, including whether it covers only formal submissions or broader communications connected with a dispute.

judgments.title: No Prevailing Party Attorney's Fees
judgments.reason: The absence of an attorney-fee provision is a remedies negotiation issue, not a textual ambiguity or conflict.

judgments.title: Confidentiality Survival Clause Should Explicitly Be Perpetual
judgments.reason: Standing alone, “shall survive the termination” does not state a duration and can raise a temporal-scope question, although Section 3.A strongly supports indefinite application.

judgments.title: Mutual Non-Disparagement May Limit Company's Legitimate Communications
judgments.reason: Terms such as “disparage,” “criticize,” and “statements to the detriment” have uncertain boundaries, particularly as applied to truthful ordinary-course communications.

judgments.title: Non-Disparagement Applies Indefinitely and Only Benefits Company
judgments.reason: “Indefinitely thereafter” and “no Party” clearly establish an indefinite, facially mutual obligation. The asserted practical imbalance does not create textual ambiguity.

judgments.title: Buyer as Third-Party Beneficiary Expands Enforcement Risk
judgments.reason: The Buyer’s third-party-beneficiary status is expressly granted. Dual enforcement exposure is a substantive risk rather than a construction defect.

judgments.title: Unused definition: Sellers
judgments.reason: An unused defined term is unnecessary drafting clutter but creates no ambiguity or inconsistency in an operative obligation.

judgments.title: No Waiver of Jury Trial
judgments.reason: The absence of a jury-trial waiver concerns litigation strategy and negotiated procedure, not construction of existing text.

judgments.title: Worldwide Process Service is Burdensome
judgments.reason: “Anywhere in the world” addresses the place of service and does not purport to displace legally required methods of service. The requested convention language is an additional safeguard, not a construction correction.

judgments.title: Inconsistent capitalization: party
judgments.reason: In context, lowercase “party” plainly refers to a party to this Agreement. The capitalization inconsistency does not change the assignment provision’s meaning.

judgments.title: Spelling error
judgments.reason: “Wlegality” is a mechanical spelling error that replaces the operative legal term “illegality” with a nonexistent word.

judgments.title: Notice Provision Lacks Email as Delivery Method
judgments.reason: The permitted delivery methods are expressly listed. Omitting email may be outdated or inconvenient, but it creates no construction defect.

judgments.title: Invalid section reference to Section 5(J)
judgments.reason: The self-reference to nonexistent Section 5(J), rather than the apparent Section 5(I), is a mechanical cross-reference error.

judgments.title: Notice Provision Lacks Email as Delivery Method
judgments.reason: The omission of email from an express list of delivery methods is inconvenient but unambiguous.

judgments.title: Invalid subsection reference to Section 5(J)
judgments.reason: The reference to Section 5(J) is a mechanical cross-reference error because Notices appears to be the ninth subsection, Section 5(I).

judgments.title: Inconsistent capitalization: parties
judgments.reason: The phrase “parties hereto” unambiguously identifies the contracting parties despite lowercase capitalization.

judgments.title: Business Definition Limited to Current Services
judgments.reason: The definition expressly covers the listed services for hospitals and physicians. The issue seeks broader substantive coverage rather than identifying uncertainty in the existing scope.

judgments.title: Assignment Rights Too Narrow for Company
judgments.reason: Section 1.B includes future successors within “Company,” while Section 5.F prohibits non-affiliate assignments without consent. A court may need to determine whether successor status under Section 1.B bypasses the assignment restriction in Section 5.F.

judgments.title: Expansive "Company" Definition Includes Future Successors and Affiliates
judgments.reason: The inclusion of future successors, subsidiaries, and affiliates is express. Potential future expansion is a commercial-scope concern, not a construction defect.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Ajuba
judgments.reason: “Ajuba” is an undefined shorthand within the definition of Company. Although context strongly suggests Ajuba International, Inc., the imprecise entity reference presents a lexical identification issue.

judgments.title: Short Lookback Period for Former Customers
judgments.reason: The six-month lookback is clear; the issue merely argues that a longer negotiated period would better protect the Company.

judgments.title: Prospective Client Restriction Weakened by Material Contact Requirement
judgments.reason: “Material contact” is a vague standard whose boundary is not defined, potentially requiring construction of what degree or kind of contact qualifies.

judgments.title: Overly Broad "Business" Definition
judgments.reason: The breadth of the enumerated Business definition is an enforceability and negotiation concern, not an ambiguity in what services it lists.

judgments.title: Customer Definition Includes Prospective Clients
judgments.reason: The phrases “actively sought” and “material contact” lack objective boundaries and may require construction when deciding whether a particular prospect is a Customer.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Acquired Companies
judgments.reason: Background C provides that otherwise undefined capitalized terms take their meanings from the Stock Purchase Agreement, so “Acquired Companies” is not necessarily undefined for construction purposes.
